get_variables_by_year <- function(year_str) {

  }

                year_str,

  api_variables <- GET(url)

  
  variables_response <- fromJSON(rawToChar(api_variables$content), simplifyVector = TRUE)
  filtered_variables <-   variables_response$variables[names(variables_response$variables) %in% variables_by_year[[year_str]]]
  
}

for (year in names(variables_by_year)) {
  file_name <- paste0("data/variables_", year, ".rds")
  
  saveRDS(get_variables_by_year(year), file_name)
}

text:
Write custom summary function

for summarizing mean and standard deviation of numerical variables and counts of categorial variables


summary.census <- function(x, numeric_vars = NULL, categorical_vars = NULL) {
  
  dflt_categorical_vars <- c("FER", "HHL", "SCH", "SCHL", "SEX","year")
  dflt_numeric_vars <- c("AGEP", "GASP", "GRPIP",  "JWMNP")

  if(is.null(numeric_vars)) {
    numeric_vars = dflt_numeric_vars
  } else {
    for(n in numeric_vars) {
      matched_value <- match_allowed_value(n,dflt_numeric_vars)
      if(is.na(matched_value)) {
        stop("numeric variables must only contain: ", paste(dflt_numeric_vars,collapse = ","))
      }
    }
  }
  
  if(is.null(categorical_vars)) {
    categorical_vars = dflt_categorical_vars
  } else {
    for(c in categorical_vars) {
      matched_value <- match_allowed_value(c,dflt_categorical_vars)
      if(is.na(matched_value)) {
        stop("numeric variables must only contain: ", paste(dflt_categorical_vars,collapse = ","))
      }
    }
  }
  
categorical_vars <- categorical_vars[categorical_vars %in% colnames(x)] 
 numeric_vars <- numeric_vars[numeric_vars %in% colnames(x)]
 
 if(length(categorical_vars) == 0) {
   warning("None of the requested categorical_vars are present in the tibble - no categorical summary will be produced")
 }
 
  if(length(numeric_vars) == 0) {
   warning("None of the requested numeric_vars are present in the tibble - no numerical summary will be produced")
 }
  
  summary_result <- list()
  
  for(v in numeric_vars) {
    
    numeric_vector <- x[[v]]
    weight_vector <- x[["PWGTP"]]
    sample_mean <- sum(numeric_vector * weight_vector) / sum(weight_vector)
    sample_sd = sqrt(sum(numeric_vector^2 * weight_vector)/sum(weight_vector) - sample_mean^2)
    
    summary_result[[v]] <- list(mean = sample_mean, sd = sample_sd)
  }
  
  for(c in categorical_vars) {
    summary_result[[c]] <- table(x[[c]])
  }
  
  summary_result

}

Now let’s construct a label query so that I can display it on the boxplot

get_label_for_var <- function(var) {
  
  variables_metadata <- load_variables_rds_by_year("2024") #let's use default 2024
  #I also checked ST and STATE variables between different years the labels are same 
  var_label <- variables_metadata[[var]]$label
  if (is.null(var_label)) {
    var_label <- var_var   # "year" has no metadata entry -- fall back to the raw name
  }

  var_label
}


plot.census <- function(x, numeric_var, categorical_var) {
  if(missing(numeric_var) || missing(categorical_var)) {
    stop("both numeric_var and categorical_var are required")
  }
  
  allowed_categorical_vars <- c("FER", "HHL", "SCH", "SCHL", "SEX","year")
  allowed_numeric_vars <- c("AGEP", "GASP", "GRPIP",  "JWMNP")
  
  numeric_var <- match_allowed_value(numeric_var, allowed_numeric_vars)
  if(is.na(numeric_var)) {
    stop("numeric_var must be one of: ", paste(allowed_numeric_vars, collapse = ","))
  }
  col_names_tibble <- colnames(x)
  
  if(!(numeric_var %in% col_names_tibble)) {
    stop("numeric_var is not part of avaiable tibble columns: ", paste(col_names_tibble, collapse = ","))
  }
  
  categorical_var <- match_allowed_value(categorical_var, allowed_categorical_vars)
  if(is.na(categorical_var)) {
    stop("categorical_var must be one of: ", paste(allowed_categorical_vars, collapse = ","))
  }
  
   if(!(categorical_var %in% col_names_tibble)) {
    stop("categorical_var is not part of avaiable tibble columns: ", paste(col_names_tibble, collapse = ","))
   }
  
  ggplot(x, aes(x = get(categorical_var), y = get(numeric_var), weight = PWGTP)) + 
    geom_boxplot() + 
    labs(x = paste0(categorical_var, "(", get_label_for_var(categorical_var), ")"),
         y = paste0(numeric_var, "(", get_label_for_var(numeric_var), ")"),
         title = paste(numeric_var, " by ", categorical_var),
         subtitle = "Weighted by PWGTP (survey weight)",
         caption = "Source: Census PUMS data")
  
}

Investigation-1 AGEP vs SEX
But first let’s use AGEP vs SEX In the AGEP VS SEX boxplot, it shows that population age is similar between both sexes, although the mean age is slightly different between 2 sexes. Also there are no outliers the distribution itself is from 0-90+ years. I expected to see outliers in this plot given we know that there are super-agers.
Let’s summarize AGEP numerical variable and see if it provides additional information on AGEP value distribution.

summary(pums_combined_tibble,numeric_vars = "AGEP", categorical_vars = "SEX")

$AGEP
$AGEP$mean

  Male Female 
213464 226293 


Summary doesn’t provide much insight into outliers. The concept that I am trying to check it whether there are any values for AGEP variable for either sexes that ourside 1.5 * IQR from the edges of IQR

pums_combined_tibble |>
  group_by(SEX) |>
  summarize(
    q1 = quantile(AGEP,0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3 = quantile(AGEP, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr = q3-q1,
    upper_fence = q3 + 1.5 * iqr,
    lower_fence = q1 - 1.5 * iqr,
    actual_max = max(AGEP, na.rm = TRUE),
    actual_min = min(AGEP, na.rm = TRUE),
    has_high_outliers = actual_max > upper_fence,
    has_low_outliers = actual_min < lower_fence 
  )

text:
Investigation-2 GRPIP vs SEX
One thing that stands out immediately in GRPIP vs SEX plot is the lower fence of IQR actually starts at 0
This means there are people who do not pay rent at all and their share of NC population is more than 25 %. Per boxplot definition since at least 25% of the population pays no rent at all, the 25th percentile (Q1) of GRPIP is exactly 0. Because GRPIP can’t go below 0, there is no room for a lower whisker to extend. It collapses to the same point as the box edge.
Now let’s run the similar checks as AGEP vs SEX to confirm this findings. While at it, we can also observe high outliers

pums_combined_tibble |>
  group_by(SEX) |>
  summarize(
    q1 = quantile(GRPIP,0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3 = quantile(GRPIP, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr = q3-q1,
    upper_fence = q3 + 1.5 * iqr,
    lower_fence = q1 - 1.5 * iqr,
    actual_max = max(GRPIP, na.rm = TRUE),
    actual_min = min(GRPIP, na.rm = TRUE),
    has_high_outliers = actual_max > upper_fence,

Now this confirms the presense of high outliers where the some population of NC is paying more rent than the income they receive. A generally recommended rule is rental expense cannot be more than 30-40% of income. Here clearly there is a segment where this is not holding true. The Q1 for all the years is actually ‘0’ indicating these are either remote workers, workers staying next door to work, and people without jobs. While mean stayed around 10 minutes, the max value of outliers has increased gradually from 2021 to 2024. This suggests more workers moving to places that are far from work locations during the pandemic-remote-was-the-norm time. However they were called to work (RTO) which resulted in increased travel time. In the investigation pct_zero column clearly shows gradual decrease from 64.6% to 61.6%
